An estimation of the $B^0_s\rightarrow K^+K^-$ decay time for $B^0_s$ mesons has been made with the help of around 37 picobarns of LHCb data from 2010. This calculation took into account around 1770 $B^0_s\rightarrow K^+K^-$ signal events and around 20 million $B^0_s\rightarrow J/\psi(\rightarrow \mu^+\mu^-)K^+$ reference events. Taking into consideration systematic and statistical errors, the result for $B^0_s\rightarrow K^+K^-$ decay time was found to be 6.85 ps with a margin of error at 0.06 ps. This result took into account 2012 data from CDF, which yielded a similar duration of 6.77 ps with a margin of error at 0.07 ps, and took into consideration the possibility of $B^0_s\rightarrow \phi\phi$ decay where $\phi$ decays to $\mu^+\mu^-$.

This research paper focuses on the numerical solution of a distributed control problem for a stochastic partial differential equation. To achieve a desired target, the problem involves controlling the mean of the solution. A finite difference method in space and the backward Euler scheme in time are employed for the discretization. The analysis yields a semi-discrete and fully discrete weak stability and error estimates. The study also obtains a more precise error bound using the concept of a weak inverse. The efficacy of the method is demonstrated through numerical experiments. The case of a one-dimensional domain is treated with additional error estimation techniques. The results can be adapted to other types of boundary conditions and spatial discretization methods.

Our findings indicate the all-sky pattern of extremely high-energy cosmic rays exhibits extensive anisotropy, surpassing expectations. Multiple detection methods employed on the vast dataset from the Pierre Auger Observatory reveal that the anisotropy degree reaches approximately 3.7%. The orientation of the anisotropy pattern is aligned with the large-scale distribution of galaxies, presenting a general preference for the direction of the cosmic filament containing our galaxy. The degree of anisotropy remains relatively constant across different energy intervals, though it may increase at the highest energies assessed. Localized anisotropy patterns were identified in the data, with the most significant signal observed near the Cratus cluster and with anisotropy degree of approximately 5% in the energy range of 58.8 to 72.0 EeV. This paper proves that any finite-dimensional Zinbiel algebra over a given field possesses a specific characteristic - namely, it is solvable with respect to a particular identity that includes the fundamental Nakayama, symmetrical, and Jordan identities as key components.

This study leverages ALICE data from the LHC at $\sqrt{s_{\rm NN}=5.02\,TeV$ to investigate flow angle and magnitude fluctuations in semi-central Pb-Pb collisions at 5.02 TeV. The analysis employs the B-field method to extract the overall and initial elliptical flow coefficients for the 2.76 and 5.02 TeV collisions. Results indicate that the ratio of the standard deviation to the mean for the elliptical component exceeds that of the azimuthal component at both collision energies. Furthermore, the slope of this ratio with respect to transverse energy becomes negative for the 5.02 TeV collisions. These findings are consistent with theoretical predictions that initial geometry and number-of-collisions fluctuations contribute to flow coefficient variations.

This research focuses on addressing inconsistencies in relational databases that contain functional dependencies and null values. Unlike traditional approaches to handling inconsistencies, this work does not require the presence of specific constants. Instead, it utilizes the properties of functional dependencies to repair the database. We have achieved two significant results: (a) we have identified the set of repair operations that preserve the integrity of a database containing functional dependencies, and (b) we have established the consistency of a database as equivalent to the absence of violating instances of functional dependencies, which is a more general concept that includes the consistency of databases containing null values and is a natural extension of the consistency of databases without null values.

This study introduces a novel stochastic model, the Poisson Autoregressive process for count data, which incorporates time-varying parameters. Unlike traditional autoregressive processes, the conditional mean of our PRG model is influenced by its own past counts through automatic regression, while the impact of these past counts can shift over time. We have derived an efficient method to estimate the time-dependent parameters of our PRG model using quasi-maximum likelihood estimation (QMLE), which enables us to generate simulated past count data that mimic the observed patterns. We have conducted a series of Monte Carlo simulations to evaluate the performance of our estimation method and have applied it to analyze two real-world datasets.

The task of categorizing objects via 3D scanning is a complex problem for AI
models to solve, due in large part to 3D data's rich, varied nature and the
difficulty of object classification itself. To break down this challenge, we've
introduced a novel concept: object representations that capture both local features
and global properties, encoded within neural networks equipped with 3D equivariant
layout information. We've also designed a novel training protocol that fuses
object features with equivariant relational learning, resulting in better performance
than existing methods for object classification and detection, and on par with the
current state-of-the-art for categorization tasks.

Using the functional renormalization group at the next-to-leading order in the derivative expansion, we have updated the position of the Yang-Lee edge singularity for O(N) universality classes in classic scenarios. For N equal to 1 and 2, the changes in the position of the singularity or its critical exponent are insignificant at higher-order calculations. However, for N equal to 3, the results from our calculations indicate a more pronounced effect of the higher-order calculations. particularly, the order of the singularity's exponent is now consistently 3.5+ε for ε greater than 0 small. Additionally, our calculations confirm that the position of the singularity is closer to 1 - 3/(N+2) than previously known.

In statistics and physics, when analyzing a random TAP reconstruction, it's crucial to understand its connection to the original energy function and the annealed mean-field approximation. This connection became clearer through the work of M. Mény, J. Martinjac, and F. Krzakala. Building upon their findings, we have derived a key inequality that enables us to measure the discrepancy between the TAP reconstruction and the annealed mean-field approximation, using a relevant norm. This norm helps us establish the non-degeneracy of the TAP free energy's Hessian matrix, which is a critical component in the proof of the Bethe functional's strict convexity.

While using photometry from stars to monitor the atmosphere may seem uncomplicated for optical astrophysics, achieving a precision of 0.01 for measuring the aerosol depth has been challenging. By taking wide-field photometry over a broad altitude range, the aerosol depth can be determined quickly, regardless of the system's absolute calibration, and even provides calibration as a by-product. Our team used extensive data from the FRAM telescope at the Pierre Auger Observatory and a similar telescope at the Cherenkov Telescope Array site to improve the precision of this technique to a precision of possibly 0.01. To accomplish this, we conducted precise laboratory measurements of the system's response to varying light intensities and spectra to counter the limitations of non-linear CCD detectors under observation conditions.

For robotic applications with high DoF pose estimation, using images as input is a common practice, offering more precise world mapping and better navigation capabilities. However, estimating large DoF poses from images is extremely challenging due to the vast number of possible poses and limited training data available for many real-world scenarios. To address this challenge, we present the DeepHMap++ architecture, which simultaneously generates a one-dimensional projection of the current state and leverages a custom similarity metric lexicographically, resulting in a efficient and precise pose estimation method. We also introduce two novel techniques called correspondence learning and projection clustering, which significantly boost the performance of our architecture. Furthermore, we demonstrate the efficiency and precision of DeepHMap++ by integrating it into a navigational system, showing a substantial improvement in maps learned through pose estimation compared to the existing state-of-the-art method DeepHMap.

We present GGLasso, a Python library designed to address general Graphical Lasso
challenges. Building upon classical Lasso methodology, the Graphical Lasso
framework, initially developed by [3,4], infers a sparse inverse covariance
matrix $\Theta$ from multivariate Gaussian data $\mathcal{X}$, under the
covariance matrix $\Sigma$ estimation assumption. Theoretical guarantees for $\Theta$
estimation exist when data follows a Gaussian distribution with a known mean and
covariance matrix, under certain smoothness constraints. In particular, we prove
that there exists a data size threshold $N_n$ for any positive $\epsilon$ and
any positive $\delta$, such that for $N_n \geq N$ the following holds: with a
probability of at least $1-\delta$, the Graphical Lasso method returns an $\epsilon$-approximate $\Theta$ matrix when estimating the inverse covariance matrix from a Gaussian random vector with a known mean and a smooth and bounded inverse covariance matrix. Our results improve existing findings in various aspects. Furthermore, we demonstrate the practical efficiency of our Graphical Lasso algorithm on synthetic, real-world, and genetic data sets.

Numerous applications in chemistry and physics rely on accurate configurations of molecular systems, often requiring extensive computational resources for large systems. To address this challenge, a new method is introduced for efficiently obtaining high-quality configurational samplings of molecular systems using Langevin dynamics. Leveraging the properties of Langevin dynamics, this new method can produce precise results in half the number of simulations compared to conventional Metropolis acceptance protocols, resulting in significant reductions in computational costs for binding free energy calculations and molecular dynamics simulations. Furthermore, the new method demonstrates robust performance across various test systems and thermostat conditions, providing precise results in line with the theoretical precision of $RT/\sqrt{\Delta N}$, where $\Delta N$ represents the number of configurational samplings obtained per second.

Our new method calculates a comprehensive centrality score for individual nodes within complex, multi-faceted networks. In these networks, defined by separate layers without direct connection between them, we can determine the centrality of any node by calculating a weighted average of its centrality within each individual layer, using a novel iterative algorithm. This approach takes into account the varying levels of importance between nodes within each layer, allowing for a nuanced assessment of node centrality across the overall network. Unlike traditional methods, our approach can effectively handle situations where the distribution of node degrees within each layer differs significantly.

Recently, we generated the $R$-Poincar\'e algebra using deformed Poisson brackets, 
which effectively replicate the Fock coordinate transformation. This transformation 
corresponds to a de Sitter spacetime. In this study, we formulate the Dirac equation within 
the $R$-Minkowski spacetime and establish that it is analogous to the Dirac equation defined 
within the de Sitter spacetime, described by its conformally flat metric. We then propose a 
new strategy to solve the Dirac equation within the de Sitter spacetime by adopting the 
Schwinger oscillator approach. This method yields a precise solution for the Dirac equation 
within the de Sitter spacetime for the first time.

The process of a sphere entering water has been extensively studied under both slow and fast impact velocities, yet the intermediate range between these extremes remains poorly understood. This research used high-speed cameras to visualize spheres entering water at a range of velocities, between 1.5 to 4.5 meters per second, with the goal of elucidating the effect of surface tension on the seal performance. It was found that changes in velocity significantly influence the formation of waves and rippling patterns on the sphere's surface, with surface tension shown to impact wave patterns in the intermediate velocity range. Furthermore, reductions in seal performance were found in the low- to medium-velocity range, with the cause determined as the delayed formation of a complete seal caused by drag-induced hydrodynamic components.

In this study, we examine how a Type IIB $N=2$ supergravity theory in $10$ dimensions is affected by the introduction of a constant magnetic field and a $\theta$-term, both of which couple to a specific scalar field. We focus on a particular sector of the theory featuring one vector, one tensor, a scalar, and a fermi field, all of which are part of a ${\rm U}(1)$ vector multiplet. Our analysis involves setting the constant electric field to zero. We find that the introduction of a non-zero $\theta$-parameter causes a ${\rm U}(1)$ symmetry to be broken at the global level. As a result, we are no longer dealing with an ${\rm U}(1)$ vector multiplet, but rather a new multiplet that contains both the original ${\rm U}(1)_R$ vector and a new ${\rm U}(1)_\theta$ vector. Our calculations using first-principles methods have examined the orbital occupation in cubanite, specifically $CuFe_2S_3 $.  Our results show that even without applying an external pressure or strain, cubanite exhibits unusual, anisotropic lattice parameters and electronic properties, stemming directly from the asymmetrical crystal field caused by its unique crystal structure.  This anisotropy results in the distinct separation of the energy levels in the $d$-orbital of both iron and copper atoms.  Consequently, we believe this anisotropic property can be exploited to create highly anisotropic superconducting materials via intermetallic doping.

A burgeoning field in quantum physics, known as discrete or driven-dynamical phase transitions, investigates the consequences of external influences on delicate quantum equilibrium. Our research focuses on the impact of an intense, high-frequency laser on quantum systems with internal degrees of freedom, specifically the excitation of semiconductor dark excitons lacking angular momentum. Using a rotating wave approximation, we find that even when the laser frequency is close to the exciton's intrinsic properties, the system behaves erratically due to the large proportion of heating (Rabi fluctuations) compared to other influences. This irregular behavior is demonstrated in the distribution of Rabi fluctuations, which are significantly large even without an external magnetic field, and are shown to affect the system's quantum state unpredictably, making it difficult to control the transition with a powerful laser.

Our investigation focuses on a 2D Wallpaper lattice constructed from non-symmorphic symmetry elements. We examine a design featuring translation symmetry along two directions and non-symmorphic symmetry perpendicular to these translations. This non-symmorphic symmetry involves a glide operation that combines a translation with half of the unit cell and a 180-degree rotation about a mirror axis within that unit cell. We then explore a theoretical model that utilizes coupled orbital waves to represent this lattice and discover its fundamental properties, particularly the occurrence of Dirac points situated at specific wavevector locations. Notably, we find that these points can be either topologically trivial or possess a mass term depending on the design of the lattice. Furthermore, by incorporating perturbations, we create scenarios in which the lattice exhibits either a topologically non-trivial state or an insulating state with a particular symmetry. These results can be physically realized in crystalline materials featuring minimal disorder and measurement of non-symmorphic symmetry along two dimensions, and our study suggests that such a design can be achieved in herringbone structures by substituting different atoms into specific sites.

Quantum states shared among multiple particles have the potential for exponential growth through the catalytic process, known as quantum-optical catalysis. This phenomenon, where a beam of coherent light serves as a catalyst, can result in the expansion of a single photon's influence over long distances. We examine the theoretical capabilities of this effect to produce coherent phases in a beam of light and explore the necessary conditions for its implementation, including the requirements for the initial photon state, the beam's characteristics, and the conditions necessary to minimize the spread of the phase. The proposed method can be realized in the context of Bose-Einstein condensates or with coherent light traveling through a dispersive medium.

In General Relativity using the Newman-Penrose formalism, the use of bivectors plays a key role in identifying the true degrees of freedom and analyzing the singularities of Einstein's field equations. This review focuses on the fundamental principles and significant findings related to bivectors within the Newman-Penrose formalism, specifically exploring their application to solve the Weyl conformal curvature candidate and determining the Weyl conformal curvature index, as well as delving into the historical development of these concepts.

A recent framework combining artificial neural networks and mixed integer linear programming for designing chemical compounds has been built upon to create a new method for predicting polymer structures. This new technique utilizes a simplified chemical knowledge base and applies linear regression to infer bond types within polymers, ensuring chemical feasibility through the use of the existing framework. A novel method for designing specific chemical compounds, as well as an alternative approach for predicting general polymer structures, has been developed using this new technique. By leveraging the existing framework, both methods ensure the feasibility of resulting compounds based on van der Waals and electrostatic interactions. Experimental results show the proposed technique outperforms existing competitors in accuracy.

Identifying tumors in the esophagus from CT scans can be very difficult for humans or computer systems due to low contrast, the varying shape of the esophagus, and the presence of external objects such as feeding tubes. To compensate for these challenges, doctors often rely on supplementary information from other imaging techniques, medical histories, and endoscopic findings. In this study, we focus solely on using CT scans for automatic esophageal tumor segmentation without using additional information. To achieve this, we developed a novel deep learning model called Dilated Dense Focus Unet (DDAUnet), which employs a unique combination of dense connections and atrous convolutions in its structure. We gathered 45 CT scans from the public Medical Segmentation Decathlon dataset and the UNC Center for Gastrointestinal Cancer Surveillance dataset to train and test our model. The results show that DDAUnet outperforms the current state-of-the-art methods in terms of Dice score and Mean Surface Distance (MSD).

Multilingual individuals frequently switch between languages when typing,
particularly when using online platforms for search queries, social media posts,
and software coding, which has given rise to code-mixed NLP. This field of study
deals with NLP problems that involve multiple languages being used at the same time.
There are several complicated issues in this field, including determining the best
language model to use for neural-based approaches, identifying code-mixed data
sets for training and evaluating models, and developing evaluation metrics to gauge
the performance of trained models. Researchers in this field are facing several big
questions, which are discussed at a greater length in this paper. We have also
included a section that outlines potential future research in this area of study.

Assessing visual description systems (VDS) is a growing area of research. Evaluating VDS involves creating metrics that compare generated descriptions and existing benchmark data. This approach is being adopted by the community despite concerns about its limitations. In this work, we argue that relying solely on benchmark data has significant drawbacks, such as ignoring important performance aspects like the quality of novel descriptions and potentially flawed benchmark data. To address these issues, we propose an alternative method that combines both fully and partially supervised learning frameworks, leveraging both benchmark and novel description sets. This approach provides a more comprehensive assessment of VDS, enabling the derivation of several relevant performance metrics, including intriguing inequalities demonstrating the superiority of fully supervised learning when the training and evaluation datasets have similar description quality. To support our case for caution when using benchmark data exclusively, we present a series of rigorous evaluations conducted on the CVC-2014 and FVComP datasets.

Tantalum oxide compounds, with the chemical formula Ta$_2$O$_5$, are of significant interest due to their high dielectric properties and versatile applications in electronics and photonic devices. To better understand the material's behavior, researchers aim to clarify its fundamental structure at the atomic level. However, Ta$_2$O$_5$ exhibits complex characteristics, displaying multiple lattice phases under different temperature and pressure conditions. To investigate the most stable lattice structure at room temperature and standard pressure, researchers have used a combination of theoretical methods, including $ab-initio$ simulations based on the phase-coexistence model and the Monte Carlo technique with effective interactions. The results from these simulations are consistent, showing that the most stable lattice structure in Ta$_2$O$_5$ at room temperature and standard pressure features Ta atoms located in both octahedral and five-fold coordination. Notably, this outcome challenges earlier research that had previously established that the most stable structure consisted solely of Ta atoms in octahedral coordination. The current findings also provide a straightforward explanation for the experimentally observed phase transitions and Hubble widths in Ta$_2$O$_5$ thin-film spectra.

The spread of misinformation on social media has been a pressing concern, taking on added significance during the COVID-19 pandemic and the 2020 US presidential election. Researchers have sought to analyze the patterns of misinformation dissemination. This paper delves into the Circulation of Misinformation among U.S. Reddit Users During the 2020 U.S. Election project's findings, specifically the impact of the Big Shift in American Politics on the circulation of election-related misinformation. The Big Shift refers to the significant shift in American politics characterized by increased polarization. The study employs a novel method of tracking and evaluating the circulation of misinformation based on users' corrections of each other on Reddit. The research reveals that misinformation tends to circulate more readily in liberal online communities rather than in conservative ones. The authors also found that the Big Shift in American Politics exacerbates the dissemination of election-related misinformation on a national scale. The project is part of the larger study on election misinformation mentioned above. The research was supported by the National Science Foundation.

Humans employ various speech sounds, tone of voice, and rhythm when teaching each other physical skills. To create effective robotic instruction methods, it is essential to understand the underlying patterns of speech used by human teachers to demonstrate robotic manipulation tasks. To this end, we analyzed video recordings of humans performing robotic manipulation tasks while an instructor provides them with verbal guidance. Our analysis focused on identifying recurring speech patterns, particularly intonation, stress, and tempo, in relation to the corresponding robotic movements. We observed a strong correlation between the rhythm of robotic movements and the instructor's speech, as well as a less consistent connection between the speech and the robot's joint angles. We found that instructors frequently employ rising intonation when referring to specific object names, typically stress certain words associated with the task, and speak at a slightly faster pace than normal. We also identified instances where the speech patterns deviate from these norms. These findings, which are validated through additional data sets, can serve as a foundation for creating more realistic robotic instruction methods that incorporate varied speech patterns similar to those employed by human teachers.

A new method has been developed for describing the intricacy of conformal field theories in two dimensions, focusing on the precise measure of complexity that must be paid with central charge when they're combined. This approach is ensured to satisfy the requirements of causality and the absence of negative modes in the large-scale approximation. When intricacy is minimal, this method reproduces the critical results from the Axiomatic Field Theory, indicating that the ground-state complexity of the trivial state is equal to its total available complexity, specifically c for the Virasoro algebra and (c,c') for the Kac-Moody algebra. All conventional conformal field theories can be systematically classified using this new framework, where the study of the Kac-Moody algebra's simplest intrinsically two-dimensional geometry reveals that the complexity of the ground state is bounded by a specific, calculable constant, thereby demonstrating that the N=2 superconformal theory and the W3 algebra's intrinsically two-dimensional geometry have finite energy dissipation.

Conversational interfaces are becoming ubiquitous, and systems with these interfaces are being widely used in various settings by many individuals. Although they have achieved considerable success, the automated verification of their behavior in relation to specified properties remains a complex task. Unlike traditional software systems, there is no established method for automated property checking for conversational interfaces. As a result, developers are entirely reliant on manual testing by skilled personnel to validate the system's correctness. This process is not only time-consuming but also prone to errors. To address this significant gap in technology, we present an automated testing framework for conversational agents that are implemented using the Dialogue Systems Test Framework (DSTF). Our system, called DeepComber, is capable of generating comprehensive test cases for a wide range of properties by drawing inferences from the system's source code, even if the system does not adhere to standardized coding protocols. To demonstrate the efficacy of DeepComber, we created simple prototypes of two different conversational interfaces and conducted extensive testing on them using 500 test cases, showing that our method is highly effective in uncovering numerous errors in the systems' behavior.

Cross-domain recommendation has been gaining significant attention for addressing the pervasive issue of data sparsity in recommender systems. Single or multi-target domain recommendations may not always be the most effective approach due to varying user preferences across domains. To address this challenge, we propose a novel cooperative recommendation framework called MAPL (Multi-Sparse-Domain) that leverages enhanced comprehensive aspect preference learning. This model incorporates multiple aspects of item properties and incorporates their influence on user preferences through an interactive process. By considering the diverse preferences across domains, MAPL ensures a more comprehensive understanding of user preferences. To address domain-specific challenges, our framework incorporates an adaptive strategy that targets sparse domains with an increased focus on item properties, thereby mitigating the negative impact of limited interaction data. Our experimental evaluations on real-world datasets demonstrate the superiority of our MAPL framework in addressing multi-sparse-domain recommendation challenges.

Hypatia is a new Julia package that solves a wide range of conic equations, mirroring the functionality found in high-performance commercial solvers but utilizing open-source technology. Conic equations are the foundation for a broad range of applications, including optimization, equilibrium, and game theory. In a typical scenario, conic equations serve as a second-layer resolution to a minimization problem, where the objective and inequalities are defined in terms of the same set of variables. However, another prevalent paradigm involves solving conic equations with variables that represent distinct entities, such as prices, quantities, and other variables. This second scenario is commonly observed in problems involving Arrow-Debreu, Dantzig-Wolfe, or complementarity problems. Notably, Hypatia is designed to handle problems with piecewise linear equations, making it particularly suitable for applications related to optimization, learning, and analytics.

The escalating use of artificial intelligence necessitates careful consideration of challenges related to generalizability, particularly during the implementation of routine processes like MRI quality assurance. We evaluated the ability to transfer learned patterns from a designated training group to a diverse set of new subjects through a novel, systematically varied protocol featuring 25 different cohorts. Our research involved training neural networks on 12 out of 15 distinct variables used to assess image quality, then evaluating their performance on the remaining 3 variables. We examined the ability to generalize across 5 key dimensions: (1) contrast enhancement techniques used by 3 different neural network architectures, (2) features used by 3 different training cohort sizes, (3) imaging modalities used by 3 different data preprocessing techniques, (4) scanner platforms used by 3 different neural network training batch sizes, and (5) tissue types used by 3 different levels of noise added to images. We found that the ability to generalize across different variables was influenced by factors such as whether the feature enhancement technique used by the neural network is similar to the ones used in training, the magnitude of the gap between the training and test cohorts, and the presence of noise in the images. Our research highlights the importance of selecting neural network architectures, preprocessing techniques, and training protocols that are relevant to the specific population being analyzed and suggests that the effects of varying imaging modalities and scanner platforms on image quality may be more pronounced.

To understand how private electric vehicles influence the efficiency of power distribution systems and ensure a stable and reliable energy supply, a new method is proposed to analyze the impact of vehicle charging behaviors on distribution network stability. The research employs a multi-agent optimization framework, dividing the system into independent components - agents are needed for individual optimization, with a central component required to combine their results. The study assumes that vehicle charging schedules are determined by individual self-interest, with optimal agency costs accounted for. The framework also considers various constraints including technical limitations of the power grid, electricity prices for vehicles and consumers, agency costs for vehicle owners, and maximum allowable network stability risk. A numerical example is provided to demonstrate the effectiveness of the proposed method.

The interest in creating lifelike meeting simulations with multiple agents has been a persistent theme in computer graphics research. To achieve more natural and engaging social interactions, we introduce a novel method for scheduling inter-agent encounters, taking into account the complex patterns of motivation that drive an individual's movement within a social setting. Our approach takes a decentralized, stateless approach, where each agent makes independent decisions regarding their encounters based solely on their current motivation, without requiring a centralized understanding of the community's dynamics. We demonstrate the effectiveness of our method in a range of scenarios, featuring up to 50 mobile agents, with results showing that it is capable of emulating realistic, unpredictable meeting patterns that are consistent with previous research benchmarks.

To accurately depict their anti-fluorite crystal structure and magnetic properties, we utilized the generalized gradient approximation (GGA)+U and the effective exchange and correlation (xc) potential from DFT+LTCAOS methods. Our calculations demonstrate that both GdSn3 and CmSn3 exhibit an anti-ferromagnetic ground state in the GGA method and an increase in energy for the ferromagnetic state when using DFT+LTCAOS. Additionally, we found that CmSn3 has a more stable tetragonal phase compared to GdSn3 at their respective temperatures of 0 K and 573 K. The J/ψ and ϒ families' decay modes into baryons and mesons from quarkonia and color singlet factors were systematically calculated for 2S, 1P, 3P, 1D, and 3D states of charm and bottom quarks in our previous study. This paper provides predictions for missing baryons and mesons within the ϒ family based on the same framework used earlier. It also includes forecasts for ground-state and excited heavy mesons and baryons that ϒ systems might produce, given the assumption that only mesons with masses above 3.9 GeV will be considered relevant for neutrinoless double electron capture experiments.

The Coxeter groups serve as a significant expansion of the finite reflection groups, possessing a distinguished role in geometry and algebra. We have established fundamental theorem for the finite Coxeter groups through the principle of mathematical induction. However, this proof is not applicable to the infinite Coxeter groups of type B. Our study introduces an alternative proof for the finite Coxeter groups of any classification, utilizing the concept of root systems. We then leverage this approach to demonstrate the generalization of the fundamental theorem for the finite Coxeter groups of type B.

Utilizing the Pantheon SN Ia dataset along with two weak lensing surveys, we re-analyze the GRB 980425 and SN 2011fe data with a new approach to calculate the average convergence through the line-of-sight to these supernovae. Our calculations yield the first probabilistic maps of the Pantheon SN Ia population under the influence of weak lensing, which we employ to determine the all-sky convergence field likely to affect such SNe. Our findings are met with limited previous data on the all-sky convergence, specifically for SN Ia events. We derive the average convergence over the length of sight to SN Ia events and conclude it is feasible to estimate this value using the most comprehensive SN Ia datasets with a marginally acceptable fit, although our results are hampered by the limited previous data on the all-sky convergence and the difficulties in calculating the Convergence maps for SN Ia events. We calculate the average weak lensing amplification of SN Ia events over the Pantheon range of luminosity and the all-sky convergence, with our results indicating that the effect of weak lensing amplification on SN Ia events is more pronounced for the more luminous events, with an estimated value of 1.17 for the average amplification of the most comprehensive SN Ia datasets.

We have theoretically investigated T-shaped node formation in silicon-on-insulator (SOI) material and explored its potential applications in photonic integrated technology. The method of etching dual-layer SOI was analyzed to determine its effectiveness for creating T nodes with air-filled voids. Our results demonstrate the feasibility of forming T nodes in both single-crystal silicon and silicon nitride, with the option of air-filled voids in the nitride layer after etching the nitride layer. This feature enables the creation of T nodes with voids in the silicon nitride layer above the silicon waveguide, facilitating self-strained silicon quantum wire and photonic device fabrication.

For our task that evaluates the context of object detectors, we use a specially created dataset consisting of 12,000 images with 72,000 object annotations. Each annotation includes a location, size, and a contextual score representing how significantly the object's context contributes to its identification. We define a context as the information outside an object that is necessary to recognize it, distinct from the object's definition or its relationship with another object. To assess the context of a detector, we use a combination of two metrics: a percentage of correctly identified objects within their context and a score representing the depth of their context. We test several state-of-the-art object detectors using the created dataset and evaluate their performance on two separate tasks: one that evaluates the context around objects and another that evaluates the objects within their own context. Our primary finding is that the context of object detectors is often oversimplified, as even the most advanced detectors struggle to accurately detect the complex context surrounding many objects. To demonstrate the significance of this finding for real-world applications, we conduct a directed attention scene recognition experiment in which the objects within their context provide the most critical information, and the resulting performance reveals an unexpected decline when compared to an experiment that focuses solely on the objects themselves. This decline in performance for the directed attention scene recognition task suggests that the context of object detectors is frequently inaccurately estimated, as the detectors often fail to recognize the level of context surrounding objects that are essential for their own identification.

The main objective of this paper is to investigate multiple solution possibilities for a specific Kirchhoff type elliptic system of equations that are given by the system of equations where $m\left(\sum^k_{j=1}\|u_j\|^2\right)\Delta u_i=\frac{f_i(x,u_1,\ldots,u_k)}{|x|^\beta}+\varepsilon h_i(x)$ holds for $i=1,\ldots,k$, within the bounded domain $\Omega$ in $\mathbb{R}^2$, where $x$ contains the origin with smooth boundary, and for a certain range of small positive values of $\varepsilon$. Here, the functions $f_i$ and $h_i$ are assumed to be periodically extended to $\mathbb{R}^2$ and are both part of a class of functions that are periodic in the first variable and have growth similar to the Trudinger-Moser class in the second variable. The main results involve proving the existence and asymptotic behavior of two solutions to the system of equations, where one solution converges to the solutions of a related system of elliptic PDE with a singular weight, while the other solution converges to the solutions of an algebraic system with a singular weight as $\varepsilon$ approaches zero.

Let's consider independent, identically distributed random variables, taking values in the set {-1,1} with a given probability distribution P. We aim to investigate how the variance of the sum of these variables is impacted by their pairwise linear correlations. Our main achievement includes two main concentration inequalities for the sum of these variables. Firstly, we establish an exponential inequality based on the Shannon entropy of the distribution P. Secondly, we derive a subgaussian concentration inequality utilizing the pairwise correlations among the variables. Both of these inequalities are necessary conditions, as we demonstrate this necessity in our proof.

We introduce the concept of a conversion, specifically a symplectic conversion, which transforms a given linear transformation into another, equivalent one, based on a set of predefined criteria including a reference scalar, a set of vectors, and a corresponding inner product. In the context of a specific inner product, we outline the process for determining the corresponding transformation, and provide examples for both the real and complex number systems. Furthermore, we explore the connection between this concept and the properties of a positive definite matrix, and examine the possibility of reversing the conversion process.

A key challenge in kidney allocation arises when more people need a kidney than are willing to donate one. To address this, the United Network for Organ Sharing (UNOS) uses a point system to rank patients in need of a kidney and those willing to donate one. However, this system struggles to efficiently match patients and donors. We investigate how optimal acceptance policies can be found to maximize kidney transplants, even when there are more people in need of a kidney than are willing to donate one. We begin by constructing a framework for understanding the UNOS allocation system and then use stochastic control theory to find policies that are optimal in the long run. Our results show that, when considering the entire system over time, rejecting a kidney is often the best course of action, even if it means waiting longer for a transplant. We also find that reducing waiting time has a greater impact on donation rates than increasing the donation rate does. Furthermore, when there are more people in need of a kidney than are willing to donate one, rejecting a kidney can increase the donation rate enough to prevent waiting times from rising. Our analysis assumes that patients and donors can be matched perfectly based on blood type and tissue type. When this is not the case, we see that waiting times will increase over time.

This paper undertakes a comprehensive mathematical examination of the word embeddings, specifically using the Skip-Gram model, in relation to the Loughran-McDonald's financial text polarity dimensions. To this end, we derive a precise mathematical formulation of the probability distributions associated with the embeddings, and subsequently, a clear probabilistic interpretation of the polarity dimensions. Further, we develop a statistical test to determine the distributional uniqueness of the high-dimensional financial data, drawing upon the uniqueness of the underlying probability distributions. Results indicate a failure to meet this uniqueness criterion for both KPCA-based dimensions. Moreover, we explore the implications of our findings on the topic of using word embeddings for financial text classification, and conclude by identifying avenues for future research into the high-dimensional problem.

This article presents the SISO-OFDM and MISO-OFDM based IDED systems as alternatives to our previously proposed optimal wideband waveforming strategy in [1].
Fair throughfall energy-harvesting and fair data-transmission are assumed in the OFDM case, and fair energy-harvesting and fair OFDM data-transmission are assumed in the MISO case.
We derive the upper and lower bounds on the optimal $\rho$ values for both the SISO-OFDM and MISO-OFDM systems.
Numerical simulations validate the tightness of the upper and lower bounds for various scenario combinations.

This research introduces a new method to model the interaction of fluids with changing phases, combining level-set and embedded boundary techniques. By leveraging the strengths of these approaches, we've developed a numerical strategy utilizing Cartesian grids to efficiently handle complex boundary transformations and high-resolution interface representation. This method enables a second-order conservative numerical scheme and has been effectively applied to solve various problems, including Stefan problems, dendrite growth, and Rayleigh--B\'enard instabilities, even in the presence of melting boundaries.

In complex multiplayer games with multiple agents, identifying stable states of strategy profiles can lead to optimal equilibria, but often lacks transparency about why it works that way. To address this, we develop a general framework for learning explainable equilibria using data and feature representations and demonstrate its effectiveness for a range of games, including those with uncertain payoff matrices.

An analysis of a stochastic model is performed, where two types of individuals, susceptible and infected, coexist on a contact network. Infected individuals can transfer their status to susceptible neighbors through contagion, but also change their own network connections to avoid infection. By examining the spread of an initial epidemic, the effects of varying the rate of contagion, the rate of rewiring, and the population's initial composition are quantified. The model shows that preventing the spread of epidemics through network changes can fail, resulting in the spread of the epidemic becoming widespread and irreversible. The rate of this failure is the same as that seen in a similar model without network changes.

Integrating various datasets, from soft exclusive processes like spin asymmetries in Compton scattering to hard inclusive ones like deep-inelastic scattering, is a challenge due to their vastly different theoretical interpretations. A unified framework is necessary to incorporate these datasets within probability density function fitting models. This abstract presents a theoretical approach for probability density function fitting, dividing relevant processes into 'inclusive,''semi-inclusive,' and 'exclusive' categories with corresponding 'process' and 'flavor' operators for each. This framework enables the incorporation of a broad range of datasets through suitable operator combinations, facilitating probability density function fitting for a wide range of processes and experiments.

To improve the effectiveness of experience replay for policy optimization, we've developed a new method that adjusts the variance of values obtained from repeated policy applications, making the replayed data more comparable to current policy performances. We've further integrated this approach into a variance-reduced version of the Advanced Policy Optimization method, which efficiently minimizes the variance of value estimates while preventing the policy from becoming too conservative. Our results show that this new algorithm significantly outperforms standard policy optimization methods when using large amounts of experience replay data.

In our analysis of conversational dialogue, we face numerous possible responses 
to any given history, leading us to present the MultiTalk Dataset. This large 
dataset comprises over 320,000 written conversational dialogue sentences, 
maintaining a high degree of diversity (a 10-way branching factor on average) 
across all of its 7 million words. Our research uncovers several intriguing 
aspects of the MultiTalk Dataset, starting with the observation that response 
diversity is significantly influenced by various dialogue characteristics, 
including the level of branching, the presence of multiple speakers, and the 
topic being discussed. To further explore these findings, we developed a simple 
model that effectively exploits response diversity to increase the effectiveness 
of our dialogue generation task, in turn shedding light on the underlying 
predictive relationships between responses and diverse dialogue possibilities. 
Ultimately, our study aims to provide a valuable resource and set of insights 
for the development of high-diversity conversational dialogue systems.

We introduce a novel method for conducting comprehensive N-body simulations of cosmological scales in various cosmological theories, specifically modified gravity models where the Einstein conformal coupling is altered. This approach leverages the speed and efficiency of post-Newtonian models to accelerate the simulation process, allowing for an enormous number of simulations at an affordable computational cost. By utilizing existing codes with minimal modification, we can quickly generate a vast array of simulations tailored to various cosmological scenarios and scales, and bridge the gap between simplified analytical models and comprehensive N-body simulations through self-consistent, high-resolution simulations. Our method excels at producing a vast number of simulations for complex cosmological analyses, such as accurately determining the distribution of galaxy clusters and the internal structure of galaxies.

Miller and Sheffield introduced the concept of an imaginary surface as a pairing of subdomains of the upper half-plane and associated Gaussian free fields under conformal equivalence. Specifically, they considered the relationship between these pairings and chordal Schramm-Loewner evolution (SLE). This paper develops the concept of imaginary surfaces further by exploring pairings of subdomains of the unit disk, and we establish a connection between them and multiple, non-overlapping instances of radial SLE. The relationship between these pairings and radial SLE is driven by the asymptotic behavior of discrete models, where discrete pairings are paired with discrete radial SLE paths via the scaling limit procedure. The driving forces for the asymptotic behavior in question are random point processes, which are proven to be exchangeable, and from which we obtain a characterization of the underlying measure as being related to the Airy kernel. As a result, we establish the independence of the imaginary surface along with its radial SLE decomposition as being invariant under rotation, and we explore some consequences of this finding. Along the way, we establish a variational formula related to the Beigel-Tessler-Wegner formula, which may be of interest in its own right.

MediaWiki's 'open-source' nature extends beyond its software, as the underlying concepts of collaborative content creation can be applied to a broader scope of purposes. WorkingWiki leverages this knowledge, presenting a platform that combines MediaWiki with additional features to facilitate collaborative project development. It addresses issues researchers encounter when using collaborative tools for their work, such as the need for data segregation from the public-facing website. WorkingWiki's design incorporates features that cater to various needs, including seamless integration with existing MediaWiki installations, customizable permissions, and the ability to centralize documents, presentations, and other file types. By providing this framework, WorkingWiki meets the needs of researchers who want to harness the potential of their existing investment in MediaWiki, while also meeting their specific developmental and operational requirements.

This study undertakes a mathematical analysis to model the dynamic interaction between acoustic waves and chemical reactions within a turbulent jet flame. A key assumption in our approach is that the flame's reaction zone can be treated as a quasi-steady, reactive layer separating high-speed, reactant-filled fluid from a reaction product layer at a lower speed. By applying this assumption, we obtain a balance law representation of the reaction zone, which includes a source term representing the chemical reaction's impact on fluid velocity. In return, we reduce the original set of reactive flow equations to a linearized form consisting of the Euler equations and the reaction zone balance laws. Following this step, we apply the method of matched asymptotics to obtain an approximate representation of the reaction zone's structure. By expanding the fluid velocity in the reaction zone near the inner boundary and using the balance laws to eliminate the zone's structure, we obtain a quasi-steady, reaction zone index that can be used to determine the inner boundary's location. By differentiating the reaction zone index with respect to time and space, we obtain a set of simplified equations that can be used in place of the original set of reactive flow equations in a linearized framework. In this new framework, we apply the Galerkin method to model the dynamic interaction between acoustic waves and chemical reactions within the jet flame. We investigate the impact of neutrinos meeting ultralight dark matter on non-zero neutrino masses, focusing on ultra-low dark matter masses ($10^{-24}$eV < m$_{\rm dark}$ < 10^-2eV) and neutrinoless double beta decay. If such dark matter exists, even tiny non-zero neutrino masses would be reflected in a specific signal in the 0νββ decay, allowing for a direct measurement of mass differences in the neutrino sector. Additionally, we examine the effect of ultralight dark matter on neutrino density fluctuations during Big Bang nucleosynthesis and the CMB, potentially leaving a distinctive imprint on the CMB power spectrum, particularly at k ∼ 10^3 Mpc^-1.

Nonlocal gravity theory is a classical generalization of Einstein's gravity theory. Based on nonlocal gravity's fundamental postulates, we establish constitutive relations that link curvature and stress tensors. These constitutive relations can be viewed as a nonlocal extension of Einstein's gravity theory. We demonstrate how nonlocal gravity connects to modified gravity theories such as $f(R)$ gravity and Brans-Dicke theory within their linearized forms. Furthermore, we provide a nonlocal generalization of the Poisson equation, suitable for solving boundary value problems in physics. Nonlocal gravity theory can be compared to its modified versions through the nonlocal character, allowing for the prediction of physical phenomena that distinguish it from these versions.

The integration of genome-wide association study data and functional genomic data holds significant potential to accelerate the understanding of how genetics influences disease and, by extension, potentially guide new therapeutic strategies. However, implementing integrated analysis across such large datasets poses significant computational challenges. To address this issue, the NIH Common Fund's '4D Nucleome' programme has made significant progress in providing a platform for coordinated analysis and a vast resource of pre-analyzed data. Leveraging this resource, we developed an efficient method for combining genome-wide association study data and functional genomic data through 'guilt-by-association'. Our approach, designed to accommodate large datasets, focuses on identifying distinct patterns of association across the genome and distinguishes between associated genomic regions based on trait-related information from extensive cellular profiling. To demonstrate the value of this method, we applied it to eighteen human traits with extensive cellular profiling data available. Our results showed a significant correlation between peak-specific alpha values from ATAC-seq and genome-wide association study summary statistics across the genome, with associated genomic regions concentrated in active, gene-rich regions, particularly around transcription factor binding sites. Notably, we found that even modest amounts of cellular profiling data can generate meaningful insights into genome-wide association study findings with associated genomic regions concentrated in active, gene-rich regions, suggesting that even more comprehensive cellular profiling data could yield even better results.

The study of subleading effects in the strong interaction is an area where the large data sets from the LHC can be particularly beneficial, given its sensitivity to high-energy phenomena, especially those involving multiple partons within hadrons. This review focuses on QCD subleading effects, specifically involving multiple partons within hadrons, and it touches on the theoretical aspects, followed by experimental searches for certain combinations of two gluons within protons and another within antiprotons, as well as the study of multiple gluon combinations within both protons and antiprotons.

We analyzed a comprehensive database of RXTE observations for all known low-mass X-ray binary systems within the Galactic Center. Our primary focus was on determining the recurrence periods of four quiescent X-ray binaries located near the Galaxy's center, which have been actively emitting X-rays in various energy ranges. By examining the observed periods, we considered three possible scenarios: the shortest period systems either have a neutron star primary with very long recurrence periods between outbursts or a black hole primary with similarly long periods between outbursts; or, if the neutron star hypothesis is rejected, then all the quiescent binaries have a neutron star primary with similar long recurrence periods between outbursts; or, if the neutron star hypothesis is also rejected, then all the quiescent binaries have a black hole primary with similarly long periods between outbursts. Evaluating the observed periods through our model showed that the shortest period systems have recurrence periods between outbursts that are significantly longer than a decade, with 95% confidence.

The rapid progress in generating and analyzing synchrotron radiation through X-ray techniques such as absorption, fluorescence, and scattering has led to a significant increase in experimental availability of momentum- and energy-resolved phonon information. This development paves the way for a more nuanced understanding of the intricate relationships between electrons, spins, and phonons in solids, enabling the characterization of dynamic electron-phonon and spin-phonon interactions. Our research focuses on utilizing and integrating experimental phonon information with theoretical concepts from many-body physics to establish a framework for evaluating electron-phonon and spin-phonon interactions based on perturbation theory. We demonstrate the utility of this approach by applying it to experimental data on strontium titanate (SrTiO3). Notably, we find that the derived coefficients for the irreducible representations of the k-point mesh capture the local and dispersive character of phonons, with the latter being associated with long-range hopping terms in the Hamiltonian. Furthermore, we show that our method can be adapted to employ phonon renormalization diagrams and sum-over-states formulations of absorption spectra, with the latter being a direct outcome of applying the Kubo formula to the dipole moment operator. These advancements provide a solid foundation for exploring the interplay between phonons and electronic correlations in materials with strong interactions.

When constructing conversational agents, selecting appropriate utterances for responses is crucial for successful interactions. This process, known as dialogue generation, can be approached from various perspectives, including natural language processing, artificial intelligence, and robotics. A key challenge in dialogue generation is variety, specifically the need to produce diverse responses to engage interlocutors. To date, research has primarily focused on response similarity rather than variety. This study explores the connection between response variety and semantic change in dialogues, using Natural Language Inference as a benchmark to gauge the degree of utterance change. Our experiments on four publicly available datasets reveal that more diverse responses are associated with greater semantic change. We also find that natural language models struggle with diverse responses that contradict each other according to NLI, and this difficulty is exacerbated for more divergent responses. Our analysis indicates that this challenge is linked to the limited experience these models have in the NLI dataset. We further investigate the influence of NLI label variety on dialogues, discovering a positive impact on response variety. Finally, our research highlights potential avenues for enhancing response variety while constraining the semantic change, and we present a simple method to achieve this by integrating a diversity-aware decoder with a latent attention mechanism as an illustrative example.

Computer simulations of massive, rotating stars have been thoroughly examined in previous research. This study extends those results to much less massive stars, with a focus on objects more massive than brown dwarfs. We investigated how rapidly these stars must spin before they lose mass due to gravitational forces, and our findings are presented in tables for various compositions of helium and hydrogen. Notably, we found that the critical spin rate is greater than expected when comparing the results to previous, non-rotating models of the same stars. This discrepancy is attributed to a stabilizing effect caused by the distribution of heat within the stars, which in turn is influenced by their internal chemistry.

For amplitude analyses in hadron physics, researchers often work with massive datasets that necessitate efficient numerical methods to estimate parameters under constraints. This leads to a need for a reliable way to account for experimental uncertainties when constructing amplitude analyses, given the typically large size of datasets. In this work, a Bayesian approach is developed to estimate parameters and incorporate covariance matrices that capture correlations between variables, making it suitable for analyses involving intertwined kinematic branches. The study's results are applicable to amplitude analyses conducted using Bayesian or frequentist methods. A comprehensive method for predicting branching ratios and asymmetries using Bayesian Monte Carlo Markov Chain sampling is also presented. These findings are relevant to ongoing and future experiments in hadron physics, such as BESIII and GLD, which will generate substantial datasets from multi-body decays in the future.

A fundamental challenge in understanding the evolution of gamma-ray bursts afterglows stems from their highly variable and often seemingly random behavior. A new comprehensive model aims to address this complexity by dividing the afterglow evolution into three distinct phases, each with its own characteristic dynamics. The "synchrotron" phase, marked by a shallow decline of optical flux, is attributed to energetic afterglows with broadened jets. The model predicts that even if the jet is not all-inclusive, it still assumes that the afterglow's radiating region is vast in comparison to the emitting region. This assumption leads to a predicted power law index of one for the radial distribution of radiation, which is then used to calculate the radiation duration in the "synchrotron" phase. The model also accounts for the effects of external and internal shock radiation, and in the "plateau" phase, it proposes that narrow jets could persist for an extended period of time. The model's predictions are compared to existing empirical evidence, and it is found that a large majority of observed afterglows align with the predicted phases, with only a small fraction showing abnormal behavior. The model's success in explaining the majority of afterglow observations provides a foundation for further study into the dynamics of afterglows.

Bipartite graphs depicting connections between distinct groups of objects have numerous practical applications, and their visualization often takes the form of a 2-tiered graph with corresponding nodes. The task of rearranging these graphs to minimize crossing points while preserving node affiliations can be computationally demanding. In contrast, our method addresses the subproblem of efficiently repositioning nodes within one component of the graph, reducing crossing points at a cost of introducing additional node placements. We establish the bounds on problem complexity, demonstrating its membership in a narrow category of computationally intractable problems that can be resolved within a limited framework of time and space.

This paper will outline our approach to optimizing bipedal robot walking using thrusters via the Torque-Aided Locomotion Suite, a framework we've developed to address several key challenges in this area. By assuming a stable, walking robot with the ability to generate artificial gravity through its center of mass, we've created a set of performance metrics that include natural stability, energy consumption, and robustness to external disturbances. To further refine our approach, we've applied evolutionary optimization to the performance metrics within the Torque-Aided Locomotion Suite. The results of our research will be showcased at the 2023 ICRA conference.

We define a new class of domains called "very good domains" which includes domains with integrally closed rings, domains containing the rational numbers, and domains with no zero divisors. For each of these specific domain types, we then identify the very good versions by proving they are equivalent to a specific property, such as being integrally closed, containing the rational numbers, or having no zero divisors. Very good domains are characterized by a single-valued property related to the integral closure of an algebraic domain, and this characterizes domains with a specific property that is invariant under extension. This invariance is ensured by a second, two-valued property called "goodness", which is linked to the total quotient degree of the domain. Both very good and good domains can be compared using order, and we establish that being very good is greater than being good, with goodness in turn being greater than having a specific domain property such as being integrally closed or containing the rational numbers. We also examine the relationship between very good domains and their affine parts.

To address growing energy efficiency concerns in mobile devices, this paper proposes a new low-power computing paradigm called HyperDegrade.  By extending existing frequency degradation techniques and incorporating new methods to further reduce CPU frequencies, HyperDegrade minimizes both idle and active power consumption in modern CPUs.  We have developed a detailed design and implementation framework for HyperDegrade, and conducted extensive experiments using real hardware and various workloads.  Our results show that, compared to standard frequency degradation techniques, HyperDegrade can reduce CPU frequencies by up to 72x, resulting in a 7.5x decrease in active power consumption and a 5x decrease in idle power consumption.  To evaluate HyperDegrade's feasibility on real hardware, we designed and built a low-cost, programmable frequency degradation platform using an old x86 CPU, and conducted various experiments with different workloads and CPU frequencies.  Our findings also highlight the importance of considering both idle and active power consumption when developing energy-efficient computing systems.

Given two linked knots, a disentangling operation aims to transform one link into a superposition of the other, while maintaining the ability to distinguish between identical components of the same link. This concept was initially proposed by Menasco and Morton to compare the number of distinct components in a link, and they established a connection to the symmetrizable Coxeter group. For classical and welded links, we develop a new disentangling operation, which enables us to define a natural distance measure based on the minimum number of disentangling moves required to transform one link into another. Furthermore, this distance is found to be in line with the combinatorial distance measure defined by a generating set, and it is also invariant under the ambient isotopy of welded links.

We've demonstrated that a specific 2nd-order Vassiliev invariant can be derived directly from the Fox-Hatcher loop, which is equivalent to the fundamental class in the homology of the modular group's outer automorphism group, by utilizing the chain map associated with the natural projection from the outer automorphism group to the modular group. This 2nd-order Vassiliev invariant of significant interest initially arose in (Kauffman, 2005) and is linked to the Witten's 3-manifold invariant and the Reidemeister-Turaev rational form. This connection to the Fox-Hatcher loop branch also leads to an inductive approach to defining 2nd-order Vassiliev invariants, starting from the fundamental class in the homology of the outer automorphism group of a finite number of closed surface groups.

In task synchronization problems, multiple robots are required to perform identical tasks at the same time. This research expands on previous work by achieving synchronization in a variety of multi-task scenarios where the objectives vary. We develop two efficient strategies for a group of robots with restricted computation and wireless communication capabilities, located in a regular network, to achieve identical completion times in their respective jobs. The first approach, via linear programming, determines optimal duration and communication periods for a subset of "leader" robots, which are then used to guide the "follower" robots in the network. In the second method, we directly establish optimal communication and processing periods for all robots through linear programming, eliminating the need for a distinction between leading and following robots. We validate our results with simulations.

In Federated Learning, participating machines share their local data without
disclosing raw information.  Due to privacy concerns, researchers often use
noisy and less efficient machine learning methods.  Although the privacy of
individual data has been protected through differential privacy, it's worth noting
that learning models can still be compromised in certain situations.  This study
demonstrates methods for attacking models trained in a vertical federated learning
framework and showcases the impact of such attacks on various machine learning
models.  The results of these attacks yield substantial improvements in model
prediction accuracy and highlight the significance of safeguarding learning models
in the same way that individual data is protected.

Kernel methods have proven highly effective in various machine learning applications, yet their scalability has been severely limited due to the computationally intensive nature of pairwise evaluations through a positive semi-definite kernel matrix. To overcome this challenge, Random Fourier Features were proposed by Le et al. to approximate kernel values using the dot product in a low-dimensional feature space, thereby facilitating efficient learning in high-dimensional data sets. However, their method relied on an unscaled kernel matrix, leading to suboptimal performance in numerous tasks. This study investigates the statistical properties of an improved estimator of kernel values, utilizing the true underlying kernel matrix and its corresponding eigenvectors, and derives a non-asymptotic guaranty for its mean squared estimation error. The benefits of this new estimator are demonstrated through experiments on various learning platforms.

Let $\Gamma$ be a group serving as the base for a right regular representation within the wreath product $S_n \wr \Gamma$, where $S_n$ denotes the symmetric group of degree $n$. This study aims to explore fundamental properties of $\Gamma$ by establishing a series of equivalent conditions that can be conveniently displayed in the form of a diagram, known as the Cartesian breakdown, which provides a clear and organized overview of key $\Gamma$-related characteristics within the structure of $S_n \wr \Gamma$. A thorough examination of these conditions will be carried out in an attempt to distill the essence of $\Gamma$ from its embedding within the wreath product.

This research focuses on conformally flat hypersurfaces within the (n+1)-dimensional sphere to explore its properties in relation to a specific geometric parameter, known as M\"obius scalar curvature. We aim to investigate how these properties change under the action of a particular group of transformations, known as Möbius transformations, and examine the constraints that a constant average value of the M\"obius scalar curvature places on these conformally flat hypersurfaces for dimensions two and higher. For these higher dimensions, we find that the only hypersurfaces meeting this condition are those with a constant curvature and are topologically equivalent to a torus within the three-dimensional space.

A new method of efficient wireless communication is proposed in a novel SWIPT system, enabling faster and more sustainable mobile data networks. The technique, called "Resource Distribution for Multi-Service Wireless Networks via Simultaneous Transmission of Power and Information," allocates network resources to services that require either information transmission or energy harvesting. To achieve optimal performance, a dual-purpose objective function is formulated that balances throughput and harvested energy in a SWIPT network, taking into account the limitations of each service and possible energy and information transfer among them. The problem of resource distribution was initially imagined as a theoretical model with an assumption of simultaneous energy and information transfer between services, treated as a parameter in the optimization equation that can be solved using a combination of Lagrange multipliers and fixed point iterations to find the optimal distribution of resources. A simulation of the proposed method in a SWIPT network showed a significant increase in harvested energy and throughput in 4G and 5G wireless networks.

Network vulnerability during a crisis can be evaluated by analyzing the effects of removing nodes from both real and hypothetical networks. A hypothetical network with randomly connected links is an ideal model for studying the impact of node removal, specifically in relation to a power law distribution of degree, which is observed in various real-world social and economic networks. Using a statistical method, we studied the outcome of removing a node of a specific degree from a random network and found that the distribution of node removal's impact (called the avalanche distribution) is directly proportional to the square of the node's degree that was recently removed from the network. In addition, we found that the avalanche distribution is similar in shape to a parabolic distribution with three-segments, when nodes of the highest degree are excluded from the removal analysis.

The detection capabilities of advanced gravitational wave detectors are hindered in the higher frequency range by the quantum fluctuations of the detector's own motion. Overcoming this limitation requires improving the input laser's stability and utilizing techniques that mitigate the effect of radiation pressure. We propose a modification to the detector's design, incorporating a liquid sloshing sensor within a Sagnac interferometer configuration. This design leverages the fluid's natural oscillatory behavior to filter out high-frequency noise caused by radiation pressure, thereby enhancing the detectors' sensitivity in the 1-2 kHz frequency range where current detectors are impaired. This innovation has the potential to expand the parameter space for detecting binary inspirals featuring compact objects with masses in the intermediate range.

Recent large-scale multiple-input multiple-output (MIMO) systems are highly effective in providing high data rates for a large number of users. In an XL-MIMO environment, the number of visible base stations is limited by the MIMO array size and greatly affects access protocol design. This paper delves into the optimization of random access protocols in XL-MIMO, focusing on minimizing power consumption and maximizing throughput while accounting for non-intersecting visibility regions among base stations. To achieve this, we leverage a new protocol optimization framework and demonstrate its applicability for a specific scenario where the visibility regions do not overlap. By applying this framework, we obtain results that show a 30% reduction in power consumption compared to traditional methods, and a significant increase in throughput per unit of consumed power.

Recent high-resolution observations at millimeter and submillimeter wavelengths have revealed that young stars' surrounding disks exhibit patterns of arc-shaped substructures, particularly in the outer regions. Using numerical simulations, researchers have found that the development of Vertical Shear Instability (VSI) in disks leads to the creation of similar substructures, albeit with distinct characteristics, such as curved formations that loop towards the disk's interior and varied morphologies of protruding spokes. By combining radiative transfer simulations with the results of VSI-driven disk simulations, we can predict the observable effects of VSI on dust temperature and continuum emission. Our findings indicate that the development of VSI in disks with masses between 10 to 100 times that of the VSI-driven disk will yield detectable signals in the continuum emission, with predicted signal strengths varying by up to 10 times, with a peak emission observable in the direction that aligns with the inner edge of the VSI-driven disk formations. Notably, the analysis suggests that the presence of VSI-driven substructures is more readily identifiable through the analysis of dust temperature rather than continuum emission intensity. The predicted effects of VSI on the SED of the T Tauri star T CrA are presented as a specific example.

The "Big Apple parameter," a new quantity derived from the ratio of neutron skin thickness to charge radius squared in heavy systems, has been found to be remarkably large in certain dense objects like neutron stars. This feature holds even when considering objects with densities similar to those found in finite nuclei. Notably, we find that there's a critical density threshold below which the "Big Apple parameter" decreases significantly in neutron stars. This decrease is more pronounced in models that incorporate dense and strange quark matter. In contrast, the "Big Apple parameter" remains large and nearly constant in relativistic and non-relativistic nuclear matter models, even at higher densities. To demonstrate its physical utility, we show that the "Big Apple parameter" can be determined using existing data from heavy-ion interactions, such as those involving lead-208. We also explore the potential for the "Big Apple parameter" to serve as a direct indicator of the neutron-star radius's sensitivity to density changes.
