This research focuses on mass media to explore cross-lingual generalization and cross-task generalization among different genres of text. To examine cross-task generalization within the media dataset across languages and text genres, two experiments were conducted: one for each scenario. In the single-task setting, a contrastive learning method known as CL is used for both experiments. To evaluate the unsupervised cross-task setting, a diverse set of nine genres was created from Wikipedia and Google's Common Crawl, along with eight genres from the media dataset across two languages. The results show that both Wikipedia and the media dataset can be effectively enhanced for an unseen genre without supervision, and the performance gain is more significant for the media dataset. Moreover, a comparison with the baseline using the media dataset finds that Wikipedia's results are comparable to a supervised approach using the target genre.

Optimizing hyperparameters in the context of differential private deep learning has significant challenges due to DP's restrictive nature and the need to recalculate hyperparameter searches from scratch for each new model. To overcome these obstacles, this work leverages automatic hyperparameter tuning through Bayesian optimization, combining the efficiency of Bayesian methods with the ability to produce highly accurate results. We design a novel Bayesian optimizer that accounts for the limited number of hyperparameter search iterations in DP contexts, resulting in an accurate and efficient approach for hyperparameter finding. We further develop a modified learning rate Bayesian optimizer tailored specifically for learning rate predictions, which we integrate into our hyperparameter search protocol. The effectiveness of our approach is demonstrated through comprehensive experiments on real-world data, showcasing substantial improvements in model performance compared to conventional Bayesian optimization and widely accepted alternative methods.

We establish a connection between the boolean structures associated with a group G and its involutions. Specifically, a boolean structure is linked to the set of involutions within G that preserve a given group action. This relationship is utilized to define a boolean structure for the automorphism group of a symmetric association scheme (SAS). The study of SAS automorphisms then reveals the existence of infinite groups whose involutions have a specific boolean property and whose corresponding SAS is finite.

A new approach to studying the formation and evolution of galaxies is being pioneered by a combination of 2D and 3D chemical modeling of stars. Using this method, researchers have re-analyzed abundance data from the APOGEE-2 survey, focusing on five elements: aluminum, phosphorus, oxygen, sulfur, and argon. A comparative study of different chemical synthesis codes has confirmed the accuracy of the results, with minor discrepancies. A two-parameter model was employed to break down the stellar population into younger, metal-rich populations and older, metal-poor populations, using the ratio of [alpha/Fe]. This model was initially applied to all elements except oxygen and sulfur, which were influenced by gas gas processes. The analysis revealed a contrasting distribution between lighter alpha-elements like aluminum and the heavier elements like sulfur and argon, with distinct patterns in different galaxy regions. These findings are consistent with previous observations from other surveys, but with more detailed resolution, due to APOGEE-2's higher spectral resolution. A literature review was then conducted to incorporate other available data, including metallicity and star formation histories, which were used to test different chemical synthesis codes and models of galaxy evolution. The results showed that the code based on stellar evolution accurately reproduced the observed oxygen and sulfur distributions, even when considering various low-mass star formation histories. A study of three galaxy samples revealed a gradient of elemental abundance with metallicity, but also showed that the code based on stellar evolution overestimated the observed

The COVID-19 pandemic spread globally in early 2020 and caused severe consequences in China, also exacerbating public health anxiety fueled by rampant online rumors. To address this pressing issue, we propose a novel method to calculate the rumor's spread speed, influential scope, and position. By applying this method to real-world data from the Weibo social network during the pandemic's initial period, we obtained substantial results. Our research reveals that the number of newly infected cases correlates negatively with the rapid spread of rumors, indicating that the faster a rumor spreads, the lower the daily new case number will be. Furthermore, we found a negative non-linear relationship between the number of newly infected cases and the influence of a rumor has on its carriers, as well as a similar relationship between the number of newly infected cases and the position of a rumor. Our study provides a reference for modeling and preventing the spread of medical-related online rumors.

A new catalog of 1066 PN in 34 early-type galaxies within the Fornax cluster has been created using data from the FORNAX3D and VLT/MINERVA observations. By comparing the PN luminosities with the absolute magnitudes of their host galaxies, an independent distance measurement to the galaxies has been made, yielding an estimate of 15.69 megaparsecs for the cluster's center and a spread of 0.35 megaparsecs for the core of the cluster. This new calculation of the cluster's distance is in good agreement with previous estimates based on the surface brightness fluctuations of stars within the galaxies and confirms the similar distances for the two galaxies, NGC 1316 and NGC 1374, that were found earlier.

The growing need to monitor complex time-series data through continuous queries has given rise to flow processing engines. Unlike traditional stream processing systems that handle one-time queries, flow engines are designed to handle periodic data streams for stateful time-series analysis. To meet the expanding use case of time-based data streams, the traditional approach to flow engines, which are built around complex event processing languages like EPL, is no longer sufficient. In response, we present a novel approach to flow engines that leverages a simple, SQL-based language for time-series analysis. To demonstrate the effectiveness of our approach, we have implemented a flow engine called LifeStream and made it available online for testing large-scale queries. In contrast to other flow engines and traditional CEP systems like NEESBAP and TSB, LifeStream's performance yields significant improvements, with a particular emphasis on query overhead.

This research focuses on semi-metric spaces, where we've established a new classification for curves with a specific property, and it includes a detailed examination of how these curves behave within these spaces. Specifically, we investigate a subset of these curves, referred to as timelike Bertrand curves in a semi-metric space, and it contains two main categories: curves that intersect the same lines in Euclidean space and those that do not. We've established and verified several key formulas for a subset of these curves, and it also touches on the concept of a pair of Bertrand curves in a semi-metric space.

The choice of loss function for a neural network is widely regarded as a critical decision with far-reaching implications, given the numerous loss functions developed to date, making it crucial to carefully select one. Despite its significance, research on the topic often omits explicit justification for loss function selection. We contend that this lack of justification reflects an untested assumption prevalent within the deep learning community. In this research, we investigate how loss function impacts performance in a supervised classification context. Our findings reveal that, contrary to common practice, using a default loss function can yield results identical to those obtained with a specially designed loss function, eliminating performance differences. Consequently, we recommend abandoning the practice of specifying a particular loss function for neural network training, instead using the default loss function to streamline the process.

This research focuses on mathematically modeling the mechanical and thermal effects that lead to the crystalline microstructure development in polymers undergoing strain-induced crystallization. The underlying assumptions include treating the crystalline phase as incompressible and considering the equilibrium between crystalline and amorphous phases through a quasi-equilibrium approach. The model comprises a balance of linear momentum, continuity equation, heat conduction equation, and thermodynamics principles. Numerical simulations using the finite element method have been conducted to validate the proposed model. The results show that it accurately replicates previous experimental observations on shear deformation and temperature changes. The model has been applied to simulate shear deformation in a PEDA sample and the associated temperature changes and microstructure development. The simulations demonstrate that the model effectively captures the relationship between shear deformation, temperature changes, and microstructure development through peptide aggregation.

To analyze the impact of external magnetization on doped Bi$_2$Se$_3$ with unconventional superconductivity, a $f$-layer was considered as part of a nematic $s$-wave superconductor, with the $f$-layer being capable of strong interactions that lead to the formation of triplet Cooper couples. Within the framework of a mean-field Ginzburg-Landau theory for a second-order phase transition, the effect of an external magnetic field on this system was investigated. A key observation was the presence of a negative susceptibility for small external fields, attributed to the alignment of the triplet couples' momenta by the external field, which results in the spread of the momentum distribution and thus a positive contribution to the magnetic susceptibility. This effect is expected to exhibit significant implications for nematic superconductors, with the possibility of it being stabilized in a state of long-range magnetic order characterized by the spread of the momentum distribution and the ferromagnetic alignment of the triplet couples' momenta.

In conventional coherent differential CPM detection, the number of consecutive symbols that a symbol can differ from is directly limited by the length of the differential sequence used. This limitation can be mitigated by employing a more extensive sequence, but this comes at the cost of increased computational resources. Alternatively, this study demonstrates how the same level of detection performance can be achieved with a shorter sequence and a delayed symbol, thereby expanding the permissible delay by one order of magnitude for certain CPM types.

A previous study introduced the concept of vacuum compressibility in quantum spacetime, defining it as the change in spacetime volume caused by a change in energy density when the source is in a thermal quantum state. This study expands on the previous work by considering general uncorrelated sources across all temperatures, employing a scalar field quantum field theory as its model. The calculation of vacuum compressibility is straightforward and can be determined from the energy density of the source. By examining the energy density, we can calculate the quantum capacity of the spacetime, which represents the minimum change in spacetime volume resulting from a change in energy density when the source is in a mixed quantum state. The study demonstrates that the quantum capacity is directly proportional to the average number of scalar field quanta in the source and provides a critical temperature above which the spacetime becomes irreversibly compressed, marking a distinction from its classical behavior.

In our investigation, we tailored a dataset called ATOMIC to examine if
neural networks with advanced training methods can successfully integrate
if-then knowledge in a reasoning framework.  To our knowledge, we've created
a comprehensive and diverse dataset that encompasses a broad spectrum of
conditional relationships, incorporating both explicit causal connections
and implicit correlations.  To assess the capabilities of integrated reasoning
on our dataset, we developed a benchmark called REASON, which evaluates a
model's ability to draw inferences from a wide range of premises.  Through
experiments with integrated reasoning, we've made several significant findings:
for a vast category of queries, we can achieve nearly perfect results by
training a simple model on our dataset, which demonstrates the potential for
deep learning in a reasoning framework.  However, our research also reveals
difficulties with our dataset, particularly in the area of explicit causality,
where both successful and failed inferences are equally likely.  To better
understand these challenges, we've developed a new benchmark called CAUSality,
which delves deeper into the relationship between causality and inference.

Linear algebra applications, such as solving systems of linear equations and finding the eigenvectors and eigenvalues of a matrix, hold significant value in various fields of study. The HHL algorithm leverages quantum computing to tackle these problems with improved efficiency. However, for large-scale matrices, the algorithm requires an exponential reduction in noise levels to achieve meaningful results. To make the algorithm more suitable for Noisy Intermediate Scale (NISQ) technology, we have developed a new hybrid method, NISQ-HHL, which draws on the principles of the Jordan-Wigner transformation, Trotterization, and the QDRG framework to enhance the performance of the HHL algorithm on current quantum hardware. Our research involves applying the NISQ-HHL method to a range of portfolio optimization problems and demonstrates the algorithm's capacity to enhance the HHL results for realistic scenario parameters.

To enhance the performance of transcribing unfamiliar speakers, a method called bidirectional multi-modal attention (BMA) is proposed for training and inference in speech recognition. Typically, only incoming audio is used to guide inference, but BMA utilizes a combination of past and future linguistic information to influence the current inference process. Additionally, BMA is implemented using both transcriptions and sequence of labels as targets for training, with the former being the primary focus and the latter the secondary, allowing for a more efficient and effective way to integrate linguistic knowledge. Experiments on the Librispeech corpus demonstrate the effectiveness of BMA, with the hidden markov model (HMM) achieving a word error rate (WER) of 16.6% and the connectionist temporal classification (CTC) model WER of 4.1%.

This paper investigates the long-term behavior of a randomly generated uniform parking distribution of size $n$, denoted as $\pi_n$. We establish that the first $k_n$ positions of $\pi_n$, $\pi_n(1)$ through $\pi_n(k_n)$, are asymptotically independent and identically distributed with a uniform probability distribution over the set $\{1, 2, \dots, n\}$ for two different distance metrics. When the number of initial positions $k_n$ grows at a rate slower than $\sqrt{n}$ for the total variation distance and slower than $n$ for the Kolmogorov distance, this asymptotic behavior is proven, revealing a phase transition at this point. The approach to establishing this result leverages the combinatorial structure of parking sequences and the Coulson-Rényi divergence. An interesting connection to the entropy of the distribution and applicable results to random walks and automaton-generated strings are lexicographic ordering are lexicographic ordering are also presented.

Measurements of superconducting nanowires, particularly NbN nanowires, indicate the presence of a critical voltage threshold for dc conduction below which coherent quantum phase slips dominate, potentially blocking conduction. The critical voltage of these nanowires is observed to be tunable using a nearby gate electrode and is found to be influenced by both the capacitance of the nanowire and its length. The results show that the conduction through these nanowires can be explained by the theory of Coulomb blockade rather than coherent quantum phase slips. The occurrence of noise peaks in the measurements of conduction, signaled by sharp increases in resistance, can be used to determine the state of the nanowire as being in a resistive or superconducting state. The condition for these peaks to appear is found to be consistent with the requirements of $\hbar\omega \gg kT$ and $\hbar\omega \gg E_J$, where $\omega$ is the characteristic oscillation frequency of the quantum phase slip, $k$ is the Boltzmann constant, $T$ is the temperature, and $E_J$ is the Josephson coupling energy. We introduce a novel video prediction framework for multiple view video streams,
which we've tested on a challenging new view video prediction task using two
camera feeds. Traditional methods struggle with significant occlusions present in
our test data due to the non-overlapping field of view. Our approach, which
employs a dual representation using a graph convolution network, effectively handles
such challenging scenarios by leveraging two distinct representations to model
different view overlaps. We collect and release a large-scale video prediction
dataset for multiple view video streams, which includes over 4,000 training
videos and over 1,000 testing videos. Our method achieves the best results on
this new dataset in terms of PSNR and SSIM.

In this research, we examine the inter-atomic spacing within M\"oser-Veselago metamaterials as it relates to magnetic field interaction. By designing a setup where two distant atoms are located within a cubic metamaterial and subject to a varying magnetic field, we were able to observe the effect of inter-atomic spacing on both the fluorescence signal and the quantum state of the atoms. Notably, when the inter-atomic spacing was less than half of the wavelength of the light used, we found a significant reduction in the fluorescence signal due to the suppression of long-wavelength components of the light-field interaction, and a correlated quantum state between the two atoms was maintained only when the inter-atomic spacing was less than a quarter of the wavelength of the light used.

The Ω-baryon, which contains sss quarks and has only been marginally detected in past experiments, has primarily been studied using theoretical methods so far. A study aims to explore this particle's properties through the study of charmonium and bottomonium production in the ΩΩ system via the process B (8.986 GeV) → ΩΩ. By examining both elastic and inelastic ΩΩ final states with photons or gluons, the study seeks to determine the Ω-baryon's properties and verify the study's results under relativistic and non-relativistic quark models.

Airborne transmission risk in confined spaces like buses is difficult to predict due to the complex interplay of various factors, including coughing distances, respiration rates, turbulence, ventilation, and how air is mixed within the carriage. We examined the validity of a well-mixed model in estimating the rate of SARS-CoV-2 transmission among bus passengers by simulating the movement of air and aerosols using computational fluid dynamics. Our results show that the spread of aerosols follows a well-mixed pattern, closely matching the predictions of the model, even at their peak. We estimate the effective distance over which transmission can occur to be around 1.5 to 3 rows of seats, depending on several factors including how the bus is ventilated. Our research supports the use of a well-mixed model to forecast the transmission of airborne pathogens within enclosed environments like buses.

Research into the interface control of spin-orbit coupling (SOC) has been a key focus for nanoscale spintronics and quantum computing. To understand the impact of SOC on magnetic properties, it's crucial to accurately determine the strength of SOC at the interface of layered materials. This research involved examining the magnetic and electric properties of cobalt-bismuth multilayers through the application of X-ray absorption near the edge (XAE) and photoemission (XPS), and found that the interface interaction leads to a strong influence on the magnetic properties and the magnitude of SOC. By utilizing density functional theory, it was demonstrated that the SOC effect is directly related to the interaction between the cobalt and bismuth interfaces, and that the strongest SOC effect is exhibited by the cobalt atoms located at the interface with bismuth. As a result, this research highlights the significance of interface interaction in controlling the magnitude of SOC, and that the spin-orbit proximity effect can be utilized in magnetic materials with inherent magnetic properties to enhance the SOC, and thus has the potential for various applications in spintronics and quantum computing.

This paper provides approximate solutions to the fractional time-independent Schrödinger equation in $N$-dimensional space for a generalized Mie-type potential, represented by the potential $V(r^{\alpha})=A/r^{2\alpha} + B/r^{\alpha} + C$, with the aim of determining the energy spectrum and associated wave functions. Approximate solutions were obtained using the Jumarie type fractional derivative, and we discuss the dimensions in which this model is compatible with the Hulthén potential and the Coulomb potential. By analyzing the potential's behavior as $\alpha$ approaches specific values, we find that the energy eigenvalue equations can be solved to determine the energy eigenvalues for the bound states. Furthermore, we derive an expression for the wave function as a function of $\alpha$. The proposed approach yields results that converge to the solutions for the Hulthén potential and the Coulomb potential as $\alpha$ reaches certain values.

We analyze how enforcing a neural network's Lipschitz continuity, as it pertains to input sensitivity, affects its performance. In order to investigate this, we developed a straightforward approach to determine the upper bound for a neural network's Lipschitz constant, taking into consideration various $p$-norms commonly used. This approach enables us to frame training a neural network with a limited Lipschitz constant as an optimization problem that can be resolved via stochastic gradient descent. Through our experiments, we found that models trained using this approach consistently performed better than those using alternative methods of regularizing neural networks. We further found that selecting hyperparameters is relatively straightforward and demonstrated the relationship between chosen $p$-norms and the resulting Lipschitz constant.

We have performed a detailed analysis of Drell-Yan diphoton production within the framework of third-generation gauge vector leptoquark models at the next-to-leading order in QCD, incorporating the effects of massless and massive particles. By utilizing the NNPDF2.3 PDF set and incorporating the impact of leptoquark mass on kinematic variables through the Lepton-Quark-Complementarity, we have conducted a comprehensive study of the influence of vector leptoquark mass and PDF uncertainty on our results. Furthermore, we have compared our predictions to those obtained using the CT10 PDF set and found that the effect of leptoquark mass on kinematic variables can be significant, with masses of around 0.5-1 TeV exhibiting a notable impact on our results. Additionally, we have examined the potential discovery reach for R = 1.5 vector leptoquark models at the Large Hadron Collider, identifying that with 13 TeV data and 5000 fb^-1 of integrated luminosity, it may be possible to detect a 0.5 TeV R = 1.5 vector leptoquark with a differential distribution of Wγ at the 5σ level.

Radiation exposure during positron emission tomography (PET) scans restricts their usage for sensitive groups, such as pregnant women and young individuals requiring frequent imaging, due to compromised image quality from lower doses or shortened scan times. Deep-learning models have made significant advancements in enhancing PET images by translating low-quality PET scans with associated MRI data to higher-quality PET images, particularly with significantly reduced doses. Nonetheless, such deep learning approaches have primarily focused on utilizing training datasets similar to their test data, neglecting performance evaluation for new acquisitions outside of their distribution. We have developed a robust deep learning framework that accounts for imaging physics and uncertainty to enhance PET images at reduced doses, incorporating MRI data, and is resistant to images acquired outside of its typical distribution. The framework's capability to handle such outside-distribution data is ensured through its robust design, and we demonstrate the framework's effectiveness on regular and out-of-distribution data by conducting rigorous experiments utilizing both partially and fully scanned data.

A linguistic analysis known as centering theory (CT) explains how coherence in conversations emerges from the connections between successive statements. This paper delves into the connection between CT and modern coreference resolution systems (CRS) through empirical studies. To achieve this, we create a customized framework rooted in CT to analyze the coreference relationships within the Queregut dataset, which is specifically designed to examine the coherence between adjacent sentences in a conversation. Our findings reveal a discrepancy between the predicted CT-based golden standard for the system's outputs and its actual performance, suggesting that modern CRS are independent from the underlying principles of CT. Furthermore, our research demonstrates that the current systems are effectively identifying coherent connections between sentences, a phenomenon that can be accounted for by a simpler, previously established method, and not specifically related to CT. Our analysis also highlights the limitations of the current systems in accurately determining the center of each sentence, a problem that may stem from their reliance on different linguistic analyses.

Recently, WiFi has become a popular choice for location-aware services due to its widespread usage. To facilitate seamless deployment, researchers have been focusing on methods that minimize the need for special hardware. Fingerprinting techniques are a prominent example, where predictions are made based on pre-captured readings of a target area. However, such methods require extensive initial data collection and timely updates to remain effective. In contrast, model-based techniques offer a more convenient alternative, but they generally require access to accurate distance information to train their algorithms, which can be difficult to obtain in practice. To address this challenge, the researchers propose a novel approach that leverages supervised machine learning to achieve accurate estimations using only WiFi access points (APs) without the need for hardware modifications. The proposed technique utilizes a unique method to extract essential information from WiFi signals before feeding it into the learning model. To demonstrate the efficacy of this approach, the researchers conducted outdoor experiments at a university campus and reported the engaging results. According to the obtained data, the proposed method delivers the most accurate range estimation among the compared techniques, surpassing the conventional fingerprinting method by as much as 43%.

The beam breakup instability poses a challenge for particle accelerators employing multiple RF cavities, particularly those used in energy recovery linacs. To mitigate this issue, researchers are exploring fill patterns that minimize synchronization between circulating particles and RF beams. However, the dependence of beam breakup instability on RF cavity design has not been thoroughly investigated. This paper delves into the theoretical aspects of beam breakup instability, leveraging a comprehensive 6D regenerative beam breakup code that considers filling patterns. It demonstrates the significant impact of cavity design, particularly its detuning characteristic, on beam breakup instability. Specifically, it is shown that cavities with constant amplitude across the beam spot exhibit more stable behavior than those with varying amplitude, depending on the beam's velocity and motion characteristics. As such, design features like built-in beam position feedback, damping, and phase shift are highly effective in mitigating beam breakup instability, with the latter demonstrated to exhibit a threshold value beyond which the instability becomes more severe.

Using the BFKL equation, we can describe high-energy scattering processes in the regime where the strong interaction plays a significant role. The BFKL approach is a semi-hard approximation that allows us to treat certain particles as being produced quickly, thus becoming semi-hard components of the process. We can improve this semi-hard prediction by incorporating additional corrections, known as impact factors for semi-hard particle production. These impact factors can be complex functions that depend on various variables, including the rapidity range over which the particle is produced and its momentum within that range. In $\mathcal{N}=4$ supersymmetric Yang-Mills theory, one-loop impact factors for the semi-hard process of two gluon production are not well established in the scientific community. Our research aims to fill this knowledge gap by calculating the two gluon impact factors for a specific rapidity configuration where the semi-hard component occupies the middle rapidity range. Our calculation involves determining the complex functions that determine the probability distribution of two gluon production over all possible rapidity configurations. These functions can be used to update the two gluon impact factors in the BFKL equation, refining our understanding of two gluon production in $\mathcal{N}=4$ supersymmetric Yang-Mills theory.

Theories explaining highly elongated polymer brush properties have provided valuable insights into the behavior of surface-grafted polymers in various scenarios. However, the parabolic model falls short in accurately describing elongated brushes on the surfaces of curved, concave substrates, such as nanoparticles or certain types of block copolymer interfaces. Previous research has demonstrated that curved, stretched brushes can be described by a new model that takes into account the surface geometry, with the added feature of a clear, excluded region at the brush's innermost portion. When analyzing curved, stretched brushes on flat substrates, this model indicates that the size of the excluded region remains constant, with its volume directly proportional to the free energy of elongation per grafting site. Furthermore, this model can be extended to predict the dimensions of brush-like structures in various non-equilibrium states, such as those formed on the surfaces of nanoparticles with multiple grafted brushes, by integrating the volume of the excluded region over the distribution of surface curvatures.

A graph G is considered fully observable in regards to a set of landmarks P if any two distinct vertices V in G can be distinguished by a unique landmark from P. The minimum number of landmarks required to achieve this level of observability is referred to as the metric dimension of G and is denoted as dim(G). However, this measure is susceptible to anomalies caused by the presence of isosceles metrics in a graph, leading to the need for a more resilient alternative. Therefore, we introduced the beta metric dimension of a graph G with respect to P, denoted as βdim(G,P), defined as the minimum number of landmarks needed from P so that the majority of metrics in G can distinguish each other uniquely when compared to P. Furthermore, we discussed the properties of this dimension and provided lower and upper bounds for its value. Additionally, we established that determining the minimum beta metric dimension for a given graph is an NP-hard problem, though it can be solved efficiently in specific cases where the beta metric dimension equals one or is equal to the size of P.

Researchers have applied machine learning techniques to all-sky maps generated by the Fermi Gamma-ray Space Telescope's LAT detector. Using four years of data, they've created enhanced all-sky maps through a two-step process involving self-organizing maps and wavelet denoising. These maps have 10 to 30 times better sensitivity to weak sources than standard maps in various regions of the sky. A new method has been developed to identify variable sources by comparing maps over a 33-day period, with the ability to distinguish sources that change over this time frame from those that remain consistent. This approach has been tested using simulated data featuring a known variable source and a random distribution of faint sources across the sky.

In the context of scheduling tasks for independent agents on a linear network, the task specification can be represented as a set of points on the real line, paired with corresponding tasks they need to perform at those points. The objective is to determine a feasible order for the agents to visit their assigned tasks along the network. This order must adhere to the constraint that if agent $i$ comes before agent $j$, then tasks assigned to $i$ must precede tasks assigned to $j$ in the order they are performed. The problem described shares some characteristics with classic problems it is compared to, namely the monarchies, interval orders, and interval graphs. However, the distinct feature of the problem it is addressing for this particular research, sets it apart from these well-known problems. A key distinction is the absence of a central "monarch" node in the network that all other nodes must visit. The problem being addressed for this research is to find an optimal ordering for the agents that minimizes the maximum amount of time spent within the network. A key contribution of this research is to demonstrate the problem's intractability by proving it is NP-hard, as well as an iterative algorithm for solving small-scale problems efficiently. The research also compares its results to existing solutions for similar problems.

We developed a method for identifying binary star systems consisting of two bright, closely-spaced stars by analyzing Pan-STARRS1 images with a resolution of 1.3 arcseconds. By creating a finder algorithm for LEO (Low-Epoch Observation) observations that utilizes images from Pan-STARRS1 DR2 (Data Release Two), we were able to locate 140 binary asterisms with orbits that have been verified through additional observations, out of which 13 have orbital periods determined for the first time. By comparing observed and calculated brightness patterns across various phases, we were able to determine the mass ratio of 14 binary asterisms and confirm the orbital periods of 11 others. Furthermore, we found that the number of binary asterisms with orbits that have been verified through additional observations is significantly lower than expected, likely due to detection limitations and detection biases against close and wide binary systems.

This research supplements the findings related to the specified context, model, and estimation methods initially presented by Auerbach in 2019. The paper's first section explores the asymptotic behavior of the estimators presented in section 2 of the Auerbach's work. The second section investigates extensions to the model. The third section applies the model to estimate peer effects within educational networks. The fourth section presents results from simulations designed to evaluate the estimation methods.

This study introduces novel versions of the Leibniz rule for the Riemann-Liouville variable-order fractional integral and derivative. It derives four distinct formulas, each representing a type of the Leibniz rule for the variable-order fractional integral and four corresponding types for the variable-order fractional derivative. It also provides proofs for these formulas.

We introduce the G4C challenge, focusing on how natural language interactions can be guided by set objectives, which can be evaluated through the lens of a role-playing game. Specifically, we select Dungeons and Dragons as our testing ground. Within this framework, player characters represent learners with distinct identities, while the Dungeon Master functions as both a guide and authority figure tasked with leading them toward a common goal. Our methodology combines a theory-of-mind-inspired approach with reinforcement learning, training a Dungeon Master that: first learns to anticipate the players' responses to its dialogue based on past D&D conversations, then utilizes these predictions to assess the effectiveness of its guidance, which in turn propels the players toward a collective goal. Human assessments alongside automated testing reveal that a Dungeon Master trained through reinforcement learning to consider a theory-of-mind of the players enhances their ability to achieve shared objectives rooted within their shared world context.

The intricate relationship between protein knot structure and function has long been a subject of intrigue, particularly in regards to their flexibility and ability to bend. Despite the significance of this connection, a clear understanding of how knotted proteins are able to move and bend through their three-dimensional space has remained elusive. To address this knowledge gap, our research developed a novel approach to analyze the possible bending pathways of knotted proteins by utilizing advanced computational topology and molecular dynamics simulations. The results revealed distinct categories of knotted proteins based on their bending capabilities, and for the proteins within the most flexible category, we were able to identify distinct "homeomorphism classes" of bending pathways. Furthermore, our research demonstrated that the spatial arrangement of knot crossings plays a crucial role in determining a protein's bending capacity, and we found that proteins with bending capacity can take on a wide range of knot types, challenging the long-held assumption that a protein's knot type is fixed and unchangeable. The discovery has significant implications for our understanding of protein knot dynamics and flexibility, and we expect it to guide and inform ongoing and future research in biophysics, biology, and chemistry.

Let $\omega$ be a symplectic form on the real $4$-dimensional torus $T^4$, and define the symplectic mapping category of the blow-up of $T^4$ by assigning to each map $f: (T^4)_\mathrm{bl} \to (T^4)_\mathrm{bl}$ the set of paths from $\omega$ to $f^*\omega$. We show that this category is equivalent to the category of paths in the group of automorphisms of the free abelian group on four generators, and further, when the blow-up is realized as the blow-up of $T^4$ at a single point, we find that this is equivalent to the category of paths in the group of automorphisms of the free abelian group on three generators.

A modified Nambu-Goldstone theorem is identified by analyzing both relativistic and nonrelativistic symmetry breaking cases using QFT. This revised version indicates that a massless pseudoscalar particle associated with a broken symmetry will always occur when the symmetry is consistently maintained within the bosonic or fermionic QFT categories, although the theorem does not apply to the discrete symmetries or single symmetry categories.

To advance in various tasks like natural language inference, users often engage in hypothetical discussions that involve exploring different word meanings.  However, these discussions are frequently conversational and hard to interpret due to the varied meanings explored by LLMs through the use of different language styles, references to multiple possible meanings for the same word, and frequent use of negation and conditionality.  To make progress in these environments, we present a new method for automatically extracting the most relevant hypothetical phrases from conversational LLM responses by prioritizing ambiguous words like "although" and analyzing contextual elements like the task at hand, the input question, the LLM's response, and the predicted word meanings.  We demonstrate the effectiveness of our approach by competing in three different environments, including the hypothetical phrase selection task itself, where our method ranks fourth among thirteen submissions to the NLP Natural Inference Challenge, but with a lower cost than the top submissions; the Natural Inference Challenge, where our method places second among thirteen entries with a 0.16 F1 score difference from the top submission; and the Stanford Question Answering Dataset, where our method ranks second among thirteen entries with a 1.3% improvement in F1 score from the top submission.

Research into remote epitaxy on monolayer graphene holds significant promise, enabling the synthesis of highly lattice-mismatched materials and reducing waste from semiconductor production. Nonetheless, understanding how graphene influences epitaxy remains a complex challenge. Here, we investigate how graphene impact changes in epitaxy, specifically between van der Waals epitaxy, peep-hole epitaxy, and remote epitaxy, on gold-palladium (AuPd) Heusler films grown on Al2O3 substrates. Our findings reveal that a shift from van der Waals to peep-hole epitaxy occurs with increased Pd content, caused by Pd-induced disorder in the Au (111) plane. Furthermore, we discovered that peep-hole rather than remote epitaxy dominates Heusler film growth, and our study highlights the significance of distinguishing between peep-hole and van der Waals epitaxy to accurately describe Heusler film graphene/sapphire growth.

A code is considered $ \Z_p \Z_{p^2}$-linear if it results from a specific type of encoding process called the Gray image of a code that has properties derived from $\Z_p \Z_{p^2}$-additive code, given a prime number p greater than two. This paper specifically explores the dimension and the number of codewords equal to zero within $\Z_p \Z_{p^2}$-linear codes for their respective general and specific cases of p. It also includes examples for p equal to 5.

Conditional GANs have demonstrated superior performance in tasks requiring conditionally generated data, but training these models is often hindered by the need for a vast amount of labeled data, particularly in scenarios where positive labels are scarce and often miss labeled. This research introduces a novel framework for conditioning on single positive class labels, leveraging the potential of negative class information to enhance both model training and inference. In the training phase, a positive class sample is generated based on its assigned label, and the model learns to differentiate between this sample and negatively labeled classes. For an efficient and accurate prediction, the model can either be trained to directly determine the assigned class or be conditioned on all labeled classes, with the comparison of these two approaches presented in this paper. Experimental evaluations on multiple datasets demonstrate the benefits of the proposed framework in both training and prediction tasks.

The GNS construction links any algebra with a faithful, positive, linear representation to a pair consisting of a Hilbert space and a representation of the algebra within it. A 2-category is defined here as the context for this connection, with categories of C*-algebras, faithful, positive, linear representations, and isometric embeddings serving as its components. The embedding within the Hilbert space space corresponding to a morphism in the 2-category is seen as a composition of morphisms in the 2-category, demonstrating the fundamental properties of this 2-category. Consequentially, the 2-category contains substantial amounts of information about the properties of the GNS construction.

The exact origins of gamma-rays observed in nearby radio galaxies, particularly whether they emanate from the galaxy's core or a distant extragalactic source, remains a subject of debate. We propose a theoretical model to account for the gamma-ray spectra observed in the cores of low-power radio galaxies by postulating that the accreting gas is confined to a disk with a specific magnetic property, known as a accretion disk around a magnetically arrested disk (MAD). When this disk is highly restricted, it exhibits two distinct gamma-ray production regions: a central area where gamma-rays are generated through the acceleration of high-energy particles in a narrow jet, and a surrounding area where gamma-rays are produced through the decay of neutral mesons excited by high-speed particles colliding with gas in the disk. By contrast, a galaxy with a more liberated disk exhibits a single gamma-ray production region: a wide jet formed from accelerated high-energy particles. We apply and test this model against existing observational data from the Fermi Gamma-Ray Space Telescope for a sample of nearby radio galaxies and quasars, finding that it accurately explains the observed gamma-ray spectra for the galaxies with a more liberated disk but overestimates the observed spectra for the galaxies with a more restricted disk. Notably, the model suggests that the missing variable for many of these galaxies may be the level of magnetic restriction, which could be determined through high-resolution observations of the disk's magnetic properties.

Early detection of heart conditions such as cardiac systolic dysfunction and valve diseases may be facilitated through automated analysis of heart sounds.  However, to achieve this goal, methods like deep learning would need to be highly accurate even when applied to poorly recorded sounds.  To simulate real-world challenges, this study introduces two novel noise models that realistically degrade heart sound recordings.  Using these noise models, we conducted an experimental evaluation of different preprocessing techniques and two deep learning approaches to categorize heart sounds under various noisy conditions.  Our results show that both deep learning methods can accurately identify different heart sounds even when recorded with significant background noise.

The proliferation of computing technology and wearable devices like smartphones and wristbands has enabled people to easily access health data including activity levels, sleep patterns, and sports history. However, training accurate healthcare models on a user's behalf is complicated by the need to respect their privacy. Traditional machine learning models are not suitable for such a privacy-constrained setting, where data remains with the users and is only used in aggregate form for model training. We propose FedHealth, a federated transfer learning framework that enables healthcare models to be trained collaboratively while respecting user data privacy. With support for heterogeneous user data, it allows healthcare models to be adapted for new users through learning from existing ones. We demonstrate the efficiency and effectiveness of FedHealth by training healthcare models on a publicly available dataset containing data from 9 different sports activities. It outperforms baseline models in cross-validation experiments, and shows that it can be an efficient method for healthcare model adaptation in a variety of scenarios.

This study classifies portfolio optimization strategies with higher order moments including skewness and kurtosis to facilitate further research in various fields such as finance, operations research, and statistics. We divide methods into four categories: single or multiple objectives are optimized for mean and variance; methods that utilize proxy values to facilitate computation; and quasi-analectic optimization techniques. Additionally, we provide a framework for future research in the form of an index called the Moment Optimization (MEO) index.

The rising demand for automated systems that can rapidly develop, maintain, and modify software has led to a growing interest in Automated Software Processing. To meet this need, researchers have been exploring innovative automated technologies in fields like Artificial Intelligence, Computer Science, and Robotics. Although Automated Software Processing shares some similarities with areas like Automated Reasoning, Automated Verification, and Automated Testing, it has a distinct focus on automated techniques for developing and modifying software. This focus has not been previously captured within the existing scope of the Journal of Automated Reasoning, which is why we believe an occasional section on APC is warranted. In this section, we highlight the connections between APC and software, present some examples of APC in action, and discuss related challenges and future directions for the field of APC.

This study focuses on a complex decision-making problem involving time-dependent costs that can change suddenly. Our primary objective is to minimize expected costs under conditions of uncertainty, taking into account the possibility of changes in costs. We have established the existence of an optimal control strategy that effectively responds to changing costs, even when they are unpredictable. Along with proving the uniqueness of this optimal solution, we have also established the rates at which its components converge when the duration of their changes tends towards zero. Additionally, we have established and analyzed a second-order PDE that can be used to determine the values of optimal policies in various scenarios.

To explore the potential discovery of rare, rare processes like lq-lq production at the LHC, especially with even or odd isospin leptoquarks, we've developed an uneven charged leptoquark pair production analysis at the CERN LHC using 13 TeV proton-proton data. Even isospin leptoquarks are identified by the presence of two jets and missing energy, while odd isospin leptoquarks require two jets of a specific flavor. Even isospin leptoquarks can be either scalar or vector particles, but odd isospin leptoquarks are restricted to being scalar in nature. Our research finds that even isospin scalar leptoquarks can be detected with an expected significance of 5 at the 13 TeV LHC with 150 inverse femtobarns of proton-proton data, while even isospin vector leptoquarks are beyond the reach of this dataset. Odd isospin scalar leptoquarks can be detected with an expected significance of 10 at the 13 TeV LHC with 300 inverse femtobarns of proton-proton data.

We analyzed a sample of 106 galaxies for which both CO (1-0) and CI (2-1) line data are available, with a focus on the line widths and optical depths of these lines. This analysis yielded a consistently high line width and a remarkably low line depth for 12CO (1-0) across the sample, with notable variations. A notable pattern of line width and line depth is observed for 12CO (1-0) in relation to stellar mass, with the line width decreasing and line depth increasing as stellar mass increases. In contrast, the line width and line depth of 13CO (1-0) demonstrate a more scattered distribution. A significant correlation is found between the line widths of both CI and CO lines, along with a generally consistent line depth for the CI lines regardless of CO line properties.
